newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian police raise alarm on poison threat.
newsitem.headline: Australian police raise alarm on poison threat.

text.p: Australia's largest biscuit manufacturer on Friday ordered all its products removed from supermarkets along Australia's east coast after an extortionist threatened to plant poisoned biscuits in stores from Monday.

The extortionist has demanded police involved in a 1991 murder case take a lie detector test in an attempt to prove the innocence of a friend now serving a life sentence for the execution-style murder of a bookmaker.
"I think this is the worst nightmare of every food manufacturer in the world," said Queensland detective superintendent Ron Pickering.

"We are doing everything possible to minimise the threat and guarantee the safety of consumers. We ask that people remain vigilant and exercise common sense in their shopping habits," Pickering told a news conference.
Health authorities have notified hospitals and doctors of the poison used by the extortionist and relevant treatment.
The substance could cause headache, fatigue and giddiness, with real danger signs being salivation, sweating and blurred vision, said Queensland health department spokesman Dr John Scott.
"If an adult bit into a biscuit and spat it out there would be no problems," he said. "But we have estimated that a little kid could ingest enough from a whole biscuit to cause death."

The extortionist laced Monte Carlo cream biscuits made by Arnotts Ltd with a pesticide and sent six packages of the poisoned biscuits, along with a letter, to Arnotts, politicians and a media organisation in the states of New South Wales and Queensland on February 3, police said.
The letter demanded that New South Wales police involved in the murder investigation of bookmaker Peter Wade and his girlfriend in 1991 take a polygraph test by February 17.

The letter claimed Ronald Thomas, 46, who is serving a life sentence for the shooting murders, is innocent and that the real killers remain free. "This is not a one-off event, it will be a campaign of attacks until this is resolved," the letter said.
Police have rejected the extortionist's demand. "We are not prepared to entertain these types of threats or demands," Pickering said.
Police have said an arrest warrant exists for John Bobak, who is wanted in the 1991 murder, but would not say whether he was a suspect in the extortion.

Police said Arnotts was not the target of the extortionist, but merely the vehicle chosen to put pressure on state governments. They said they feared other food companies may become involved in the extortion.
Arnotts is about 70 percent owned by U.S. food processing giant Campbell Soup Co. "I stress that Arnotts is an innocent victim in this threat," Pickering said.
"It is not only Arnotts that we would be concerned about," he said, adding that the poisoned biscuits were not laced in the production process, but after being bought by the extortionist.
Health official Scott said the laced biscuits had been carefully taken apart and the unnamed pesticide mixed with a vegetable dye and the cream filling and then reassembled.

Arnotts said it had decided to recall all its products from the east coast states of New South Wales and Queensland. "That decision was not taken lightly and by God I wish I did not have to take it," said Chris Roberts, Arnotts's managing director.
However, Roberts said he believed all Arnotts products on supermarket shelves and now in homes were safe.
"On all the evidence there will be no threat to products until the 17th of this month, which is next Monday," he said.
Australia's first major extortion case involving food was reported in 1985 when Edward Dowling was sentenced to 20 years in jail for lacing baby food with caustic soda.

The country has seen a series of extortion threats since, with extortionists poisoning baby food, putting cyanide in toothpaste, lacing pineapple with arsenic, putting needles in pies, syringes in soft drinks and sewing needles in potato chip packets. All of the extortion attempts failed.
